### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to establish whether differential privacy (DP) can protect eigenspectrum-based hallucination monitor logs while preserving utility. None of the prior papers explicitly address the same objective. While several papers (e.g., [1], [2], [19]) discuss DP in spectral analysis or eigenspectrum-related tasks, none focus on eigenspectrum-based hallucination monitoring or its specific privacy-utility tradeoff. Papers like [12] and [14] address DP for anomaly detection but do not target eigenspectrum-based hallucination monitoring.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves the first evaluation of DP for eigenspectrum-based hallucination detection using a pre-registered privacy-utility tradeoff framework with explicit decision criteria. Papers [8], [9], [11], and [27] discuss privacy-utility tradeoffs in DP, but none apply this framework to eigenspectrum-based hallucination detection. Papers [1], [2], and [19] address DP in spectral analysis but do not use a pre-registered privacy-utility tradeoff framework with explicit decision criteria. Thus, the mechanism is not substantively equivalent to any prior work.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses a pre-registered viability threshold framework (5-point AUROC drop) applied at epsilon=5, delta=10^-5. Papers [8], [9], [11], and [27] discuss privacy-utility tradeoffs and evaluation frameworks for DP, including statistical thresholds and tradeoff analysis. While the specific threshold and parameters differ, the evaluation design (privacy-utility tradeoff framework) is substantively equivalent to these prior works. Therefore, the evaluation facet is covered.

### Domain
The domain is differential privacy for LLM hallucination monitoring. None of the prior papers address DP specifically for LLM hallucination monitoring. Papers like [12], [14], and [15] discuss DP for anomaly detection in other domains (e.g., energy markets, social networks), but these are distinct application areas. Thus, the domain is uncovered.
